Rust at work, part 1 of 4

Your first two weeks at Kettle Creek Supply

You have just started at Kettle Creek Supply, a distributor of bearings, bolts, hoses and other industrial parts. Your title says analyst. The job is writing software. Your manager will email you work, and each request needs a little more Rust than the last. This page teaches exactly that much, just before you need it. You write all the code yourself, in your own editor. When a ticket is done, a senior engineer reviews it the way a pull request is reviewed at a well-run company: what is wrong, what is unclear, and what will hurt in six months.

What you need. Rust 1.89 or newer (cargo --version), git, Neovim with the Rust setup you already have, an internet connection for the first build, and the practice database learning/data/kettle_creek.db from this folder.

What you have at the end of part 1. A tested Rust codebase of five or six hundred lines, split into modules, that you wrote and can defend line by line. It reads the warehouse database, reconciles invoices against purchase orders, parses dirty data without crashing, and produces the monthly Excel pack for finance. Every program, output and compiler error on this page was run before it was written down.

How to work a ticket.

  1. Read the email. Before scrolling, write three lines in your journal: what you think the program needs to do, and what you don't know how to do yet.
  2. Read the wiki page under it. That is the "just enough Rust" for this ticket. Type the examples, don't paste them: your fingers learn shapes that your eyes skim over.
  3. Do the warm-up drills. They take about fifteen minutes and use the real database.
  4. Build the ticket. Open a hint only after twenty minutes of being properly stuck.
  5. Run the sanity checks, commit, and ask for a review.
  6. Fix what the review finds, yourself. Then read "Under the hood" and "Go deeper" when you want more.

How this works

Kettle Creek Supply buys parts from two dozen suppliers and sells them to factories and repair shops. Purchasing raises a purchase order (PO) for each order: what it bought, how many and at what price. The supplier ships the parts and later sends an invoice, which says how much to pay. Most of the work in this course comes from a single question that every distributor asks: did we pay what we agreed to pay?

The company is invented and so is every row of its data. The work is real. Reconciling invoices, cleaning a newly acquired branch's records, building a scheduled job and putting an API in front of it are things people get paid to do, and they need the same skills here as they do in a real job.

Who's who

WhoWhat they want from you
Dana Whitlock, Operations ManagerYour manager. Writes the tickets. Cares whether the answer is right and on time, not how the code looks.
Priya Raman, Accounts Payable leadFinance. Pays the suppliers. Cares about every cent, and appears from ticket 2.
The senior engineerReviews your code when a ticket is done. In practice this is Claude, run from your terminal, under rules that stop it writing your code. See How reviews work.

House rules

These are the rules a good engineering team would give a new hire. Each one is here because breaking it costs you something later.

  1. You write every line. Claude can explain a compiler error, point you at a concept, or review finished work. It does not write your implementation. The CLAUDE.md you add on day one tells it so.
  2. SQL stops at SELECT columns FROM table. No WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY or SUM. Kettle Creek's IT team asks for this because business rules buried in SQL strings inside a program are easy to miss in review, awkward to test without a live database, and soon forgotten. For you there is a second reason: every filter, join and total you write in Rust is Rust you learn.
  3. No crate until a ticket needs it. Each ticket names the crates it allows. Learning what the standard library already does is part of the job.
  4. Clean before review. cargo fmt, then cargo clippy --all-targets with no warnings, then cargo test. A reviewer's time goes on design, not on things a tool can find.
  5. Commit each ticket, and say why. A commit message says what changed and why it changed. Tag the commit you hand in, so the review can see exactly what changed since the last ticket.
  6. Keep a journal. Three lines per ticket in JOURNAL.md: what surprised you, what the compiler taught you, and what you would design differently. Writing it down is what turns an error you fixed into one you won't make again.

The whole road

The codebase grows with you. You won't design a big system up front; each new request pushes the existing code until it needs a better shape, and that's when you learn the shape. Part 1 is written and on this page. Later parts get written when you reach them, so they can push on whatever your reviews show you need.

Day one: set up

Most of this you already have. The point of today is a project you can build, a loop you can run in your sleep, and the rules written down where Claude will read them.

Check your tools

cargo --version
rustup component list --installed

You want cargo 1.89 or newer (rustup update gets it) and, in the component list, clippy, rustfmt and rust-analyzer. On this machine all three are installed.

Make the project

cd ~/projects
cargo new kettle_creek
cd kettle_creek
mkdir data out
cp ~/projects/space_sim/learning/data/kettle_creek.db data/
cargo add rusqlite --features bundled
printf '/out\n/data/*.db\n' >> .gitignore

cargo new makes Cargo.toml, src/main.rs and a git repository with a .gitignore that already skips target/. The last line adds two more: your program's output files, which are rebuilt every run, and your copy of the database, which you can always copy again.

cargo add rusqlite --features bundled adds the SQLite crate. A crate is one unit of compiled Rust, a library or a program, and a package is what cargo downloads and builds, holding one or more crates. Day to day, people say crate for both. bundled compiles SQLite itself from C source into your program, so nothing has to be installed on the machine. That makes the first build slow, a minute or so, and every build after it fast. Cargo.toml now ends with something like:

[dependencies]
rusqlite = { version = "0.40.2", features = ["bundled"] }

Your version may be newer. If an example on this page stops compiling with a newer rusqlite, pin the tested one with version = "=0.40.2".

The database

The file is a copy of the warehouse system's tables, as of Monday, October 5, 2026. Dates are text in YYYY-MM-DD form. Money is stored the way many real systems store it, as floating-point dollars in a REAL column, and ticket 3 is about why that is a problem.

TableRowsColumns
suppliers24supplier_id, name, city, state, payment_terms_days, active (1 or 0)
products176sku, description, category, supplier_id, list_price
purchase_orders2,017po_id, supplier_id, branch (MAIN or MILLBROOK), buyer, order_date, expected_date, received_date (empty until the parts arrive), status (open, received or cancelled)
po_lines5,315po_id, line_no, sku, quantity, unit_price
invoices1,745invoice_id, invoice_number, supplier_id, po_id, invoice_date, amount
branch_invoices183All text, no rules. You meet it in ticket 4.

To look around, sqlite3 data/kettle_creek.db opens a prompt. .tables lists tables, .schema purchase_orders shows one, and SELECT * FROM suppliers LIMIT 5; shows a few rows. Using SQL to look is fine. The rule is about what goes in your program.

The loop you'll run a thousand times

CommandWhat it doesPython's nearest
cargo checkType-checks without building a program. Fastest way to see errors.Running mypy
cargo runBuilds, then runs src/main.rs. Arguments after -- go to your program.python main.py
cargo clippy --all-targetsThe linter: hundreds of checks for code that works but could be clearer, faster or more correct.ruff or pylint
cargo fmtFormats every file the one standard way. Nobody argues about style in Rust.black
cargo testBuilds and runs every test. From ticket 4.pytest

Your editor

Your Neovim already runs rust-analyzer through rustaceanvim, with clippy on every save, and shows inferred types as gray inlay hints. Start nvim from the project folder so it picks up the right project. The keys worth learning this week, all from your own config:

KeyWhat it does
KHover: the type and docs of whatever is under the cursor. Use it constantly.
gdGo to definition, including into a crate's source. Reading library code is how you learn idioms.
<leader>cdShow this line's problems in a float.
<leader>rdThe full compiler message, laid out the way cargo build prints it. Read this rather than the one-line summary.
<leader>reExplain the error code, the same text as rustc --explain.
<leader>roOpen the docs page for the symbol under the cursor.
<leader>rr, <leader>rtRun the program, run tests.
<leader>xxEvery problem in the project, as a list.

How to read a compiler error

Rust's compiler is the best teacher you'll have, if you read what it says. Here is a small mistake and the message it produces:

fn main() {
    let words = vec!["pear", "fig"];
    words.push("kiwi");
    println!("{words:?}");
}
error[E0596]: cannot borrow `words` as mutable, as it is not declared as mutable
 --> src/main.rs:3:5
  |
3 |     words.push("kiwi");
  |     ^^^^^ cannot borrow as mutable
  |
help: consider changing this to be mutable
  |
2 |     let mut words = vec!["pear", "fig"];
  |         +++

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0596`.
error: could not compile `kettle_creek` (bin "kettle_creek") due to 1 previous error
  • The first line is the headline: an error code (E0596) and a sentence. The code is a search term: rustc --explain E0596 prints a page about it with examples.
  • The arrow (--> src/main.rs:3:5) is the file, line and column.
  • The carets (^^^^^) underline the exact code, with a label saying what is wrong there.
  • The help is a suggested fix, and the +++ marks what it would add. It is right most of the time. When it isn't, it still tells you what the compiler expected.

Fix the first error, then rebuild. One mistake often causes several errors further down, and they disappear with the first.

Tell Claude the rules

Save this as CLAUDE.md in the project root. Claude Code reads it at the start of every session in that folder, so the rules hold even when you ask for help late at night and would secretly like the answer.

# kettle_creek

My Rust learning project. I am working through the guide at
~/projects/space_sim/learning/rust_at_work.html, one ticket at a time.

## Rules for Claude

- Never write or edit code in this project, even if I ask casually.
  Never show me a full solution to a ticket.
- If I'm stuck, ask what I tried, then give the smallest hint that
  unblocks me: a concept name, a docs link, or a short example on
  different data. Suggest the next rung of the guide's hint ladder
  before going further.
- Explaining compiler errors is encouraged: what the message means and
  what Rust is protecting me from. Let me write the fix.
- When I ask for a senior review, follow "How reviews work" in the
  guide: run the checks, compare my output with the answer key, then
  review like a senior engineer on a pull request. Don't rewrite it.
- The answer key is in ~/projects/testRandomShiz/rust_at_work/answer_key.
  Never show me its code or open its output files for me. You may compare
  my output with it and tell me where they differ.

Then start the journal and make the first commit:

printf '# Journal\n\n' > JOURNAL.md
cargo run
git add -A
git commit -m "Start kettle_creek: empty binary, rusqlite, rules for Claude"

If cargo run prints Hello, world! after compiling SQLite, day one is done.

How reviews work

A review is where most of the learning in this course happens. Getting a program to print the right number is half the job. The other half is a program that the next person, or you in six months, can read, change and trust. Nobody can teach you that half from a book. It comes from someone looking at your code and asking why.

When to ask

When the sanity checks pass, cargo fmt and cargo clippy --all-targets are clean, and the work is committed and tagged:

git add -A
git commit -m "Ticket 1: count open POs and list stale ones"
git tag t1-submitted

What to paste

Start claude in the project folder and paste this, with the ticket number filled in. Each ticket adds a line or two of its own to focus the review.

Senior review, ticket N.

My code is in this folder; the tag tN-submitted is what I'm handing in,
and the ticket is the "Ticket N" section of
~/projects/space_sim/learning/rust_at_work.html.

1. Run cargo fmt --check, cargo clippy --all-targets and cargo test,
   then run the program the way the ticket asks.
2. Compare my output files with the answer key's
   (~/projects/testRandomShiz/rust_at_work/answer_key/out/tN/).
   Tell me whether they match. If not, tell me which rows or numbers
   differ, but not why. Free-text columns (like a reject reason) only
   have to mean the same thing, not match word for word.
3. Review it like a senior engineer reviewing a pull request:
   correctness, structure and file layout, naming, error handling,
   ownership, idiomatic Rust and tests. At most seven points, most
   important first. For each one: file and line, what's wrong, why it
   matters, and the concept or docs page to look up.
4. Don't rewrite my code or show me a fixed version. A short example on
   different data is fine.
5. End with one thing I did well, and one question for my journal.

What the reviewer looks for

The same list every time. Read it before you start a ticket, not just before you hand it in.

AreaThe question
CorrectDoes it do what the ticket says, including the edge cases the email mentions in passing?
ClearDoes main read like a summary of the program? Does each function do one thing its name describes?
StructuredIs each file about one thing? Is the structure as simple as the problem allows, and no simpler?
Honest about failureCan bad data or a missing file crash it? When it fails, does the message say what went wrong and where?
OwnershipDoes it borrow by default, and clone only on purpose?
IdiomaticIterators where they read better than loops, the standard library's types instead of homemade ones, derive instead of hand-written boilerplate.
TestedFrom ticket 4: would a test fail if the important logic broke?
ReproducibleSame input, same output, byte for byte. No absolute paths baked in.

After the review

Fix what it found, yourself. If you disagree with a point, say so and ask for the tradeoff. A good reviewer can tell you what the alternative costs, and sometimes your way is fine. Then write your journal lines, commit, and git tag tN-final. The next ticket starts from there.

Ticket 1: open purchase orders

From
Dana Whitlock, Operations Manager
To

Date
Monday, October 5, 2026, 8:12 AM
Subject
Open POs, a quick one for your first day

Welcome aboard. Glad you're here.

First thing. Purchasing thinks we have a pile of POs still marked open that actually arrived months ago and nobody closed out. They make our committed-spend number look worse than it is. Can you tell me:

  1. How many POs are open right now.
  2. Which open POs were ordered before August 6, so more than 60 days ago. Send those as stale_open_pos.csv with columns po_id, supplier_id, buyer and order_date, oldest first. Supplier IDs are fine for now.

Everything's in kettle_creek.db, table purchase_orders. You know IT's rule: plain SELECTs to pull the table, logic in the program. There's a wiki page on reading the database, here.

End of day tomorrow is fine.

Dana

This ticket teaches structs, Vec, iterators and closures, borrowing, Result and ?, sorting and writing a file. Under the hood: the stack and the heap, and why ISO dates sort as text. Crates allowed: rusqlite.

Engineering wiki / Rust / Reading the database

From a table to a Vec

Every program in Part 1 has the same three steps: load rows into Rust values, work on them in Rust, write the result. This page covers all three. The examples use a tiny lending library rather than our own tables, so you can try things without touching real data. The shapes carry straight over.

The practice library database

The examples import it as snippets::library, so make a scratch project with that name, next to kettle_creek:

cd ~/projects
cargo new snippets
cd snippets
cargo add rusqlite --features bundled

Save the code below as src/lib.rs, beside the src/main.rs that cargo new made. A package can hold a library and a program at once, and the program reaches the library by the package's name. Then type an example into src/main.rs and cargo run. The database is built in memory each run, so nothing is saved.

use rusqlite::{Connection, Result};

/// A tiny lending library, built in memory, for trying things out.
pub fn library() -> Result<Connection> {
    let db = Connection::open_in_memory()?;
    db.execute_batch(
        "CREATE TABLE books (
             book_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
             title   TEXT NOT NULL,
             author  TEXT NOT NULL
         );
         CREATE TABLE loans (
             loan_id     INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
             book_id     INTEGER NOT NULL,
             member      TEXT NOT NULL,
             loaned_on   TEXT NOT NULL,
             returned_on TEXT,
             status      TEXT NOT NULL
         );
         CREATE TABLE fines (
             loan_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
             amount  REAL NOT NULL
         );
         INSERT INTO books VALUES
             (101, 'The Mythical Man-Month', 'Brooks'),
             (102, 'Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs', 'Abelson'),
             (103, 'The Art of Computer Programming', 'Knuth'),
             (104, 'A Discipline of Programming', 'Dijkstra'),
             (105, 'Notes on the Synthesis of Form', 'Alexander');
         INSERT INTO loans VALUES
             (1, 101, 'Ada',    '2026-08-03', '2026-08-20', 'returned'),
             (2, 102, 'Grace',  '2026-08-11', NULL,         'out'),
             (3, 103, 'Alan',   '2026-09-01', NULL,         'out'),
             (4, 101, 'Grace',  '2026-09-02', '2026-09-15', 'returned'),
             (5, 104, 'Edsger', '2026-09-28', NULL,         'out'),
             (6, 105, 'Ada',    '2026-07-19', NULL,         'lost'),
             (7, 103, 'Grace',  '2026-07-30', '2026-08-29', 'returned');
         INSERT INTO fines VALUES
             (1, 0.10), (1, 0.20), (4, 0.30), (6, 24.95), (7, 0.70), (7, 0.10);",
    )?;
    Ok(db)
}

Describe a row with a struct

A struct is a named group of fields, each with a type. It is Python's @dataclass, except the types are checked when the program is compiled rather than ignored.

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Loan {
    loan_id: i64,
    member: String,
    loaned_on: String,
    returned_on: Option<String>,
    status: String,
}

Pick each field's type from the column:

  • INTEGER becomes i64, a 64-bit signed integer. SQLite's integers are 64-bit, so i64 always fits.
  • TEXT becomes String: text that the struct owns. You'll see its cousin &str in a moment.
  • A column that can be NULL becomes Option<T>. Option<String> is either Some(text) or None. Rust has no null, so a missing value has to be visible in the type, and the compiler makes you handle it before you use it.

#[derive(Debug)] asks the compiler to write the code that prints the struct with {:?}. Making one and printing it:

let loan = Loan {
    loan_id: 2,
    member: String::from("Grace"),
    loaned_on: "2026-08-11".to_string(),
    returned_on: None,
    status: "out".to_string(),
};
println!("{} borrowed on {}", loan.member, loan.loaned_on);
println!("{:?}", loan);
println!("{loan:#?}");
Grace borrowed on 2026-08-11
Loan { loan_id: 2, member: "Grace", loaned_on: "2026-08-11", returned_on: None, status: "out" }
Loan {
    loan_id: 2,
    member: "Grace",
    loaned_on: "2026-08-11",
    returned_on: None,
    status: "out",
}

"2026-08-11" on its own is a &str, a borrowed view of text that's baked into the program. A struct field of type String needs text it owns, so .to_string() or String::from(...) makes an owned copy. {:#?} is the pretty, multi-line form of {:?}.

Load the rows

Here is the whole load step, with main:

use rusqlite::Connection;
use snippets::library;
use std::error::Error;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Loan {
    loan_id: i64,
    member: String,
    loaned_on: String,
    returned_on: Option<String>,
    status: String,
}

fn load_loans(db: &Connection) -> rusqlite::Result<Vec<Loan>> {
    let mut stmt =
        db.prepare("SELECT loan_id, member, loaned_on, returned_on, status FROM loans")?;
    let rows = stmt.query_map([], |row| {
        Ok(Loan {
            loan_id: row.get(0)?,
            member: row.get(1)?,
            loaned_on: row.get(2)?,
            returned_on: row.get(3)?,
            status: row.get(4)?,
        })
    })?;
    rows.collect()
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let db = library()?;
    let loans = load_loans(&db)?;
    println!("loaded {} loans", loans.len());
    for loan in &loans {
        println!(
            "{} {:<6} {} {:?} {}",
            loan.loan_id, loan.member, loan.loaned_on, loan.returned_on, loan.status
        );
    }
    Ok(())
}
loaded 7 loans
1 Ada    2026-08-03 Some("2026-08-20") returned
2 Grace  2026-08-11 None out
3 Alan   2026-09-01 None out
4 Grace  2026-09-02 Some("2026-09-15") returned
5 Edsger 2026-09-28 None out
6 Ada    2026-07-19 None lost
7 Grace  2026-07-30 Some("2026-08-29") returned

Line by line:

  • db.prepare(...) compiles the SQL once and gives back a statement. It can fail (a typo in the SQL, say), so it returns a Result, and the ? passes any error up to the caller.
  • stmt.query_map([], |row| ...) runs the query and calls the closure |row| ... once per row. A closure is an inline function, like Python's lambda but allowed to be as long as you like. The [] means "no parameters".
  • row.get(0)? reads column 0 and converts it to whatever type the field needs. The compiler works out the type from the struct field. If the conversion fails, for example a NULL going into a String, you get an error, not a silent empty string.
  • rows.collect() runs through every row and gathers the results. The function's return type, rusqlite::Result<Vec<Loan>>, tells collect what to build: either every row in a Vec, or the first error.
  • fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> lets main use ? too. On success it returns Ok(()), where () is Rust's "nothing". On failure it returns any kind of error, and Rust prints it and exits with a failure code. For a program this size, that is enough error handling. Ticket 4 does better.

Your own database file

The examples use library(). Your program opens the real file instead, by a path relative to the folder you run cargo run from:

let db = Connection::open("data/kettle_creek.db")?;
let n: i64 = db.query_row("SELECT count(*) FROM suppliers", [], |row| row.get(0))?;
println!("{n} suppliers");
24 suppliers

(query_row is for a query that returns exactly one row. It's here to keep the example short. Your loaders use query_map.) One trap: Connection::open creates an empty database if the file doesn't exist, so a typo in the path doesn't fail where you made it. It fails later, and confusingly:

let db = Connection::open("data_kettle_creek.db")?; // typo: _ for /
let result = db.prepare("SELECT supplier_id, name FROM suppliers");
println!("{:?}", result.err().map(|e| e.to_string()));
Some("no such table: suppliers")

Opening read-only refuses a missing file at once, with the path in the message, and it guarantees your program can't change the warehouse data:

let flags = OpenFlags::SQLITE_OPEN_READ_ONLY;
let result = Connection::open_with_flags("data_kettle_creek.db", flags);
println!("{:?}", result.err().map(|e| e.to_string()));
Some("unable to open database file: data_kettle_creek.db")

Forget main's return type and you get one of the most common errors there is:

fn main() {
    let count: i64 = "70".parse()?;
    println!("{count}");
}
error[E0277]: the `?` operator can only be used in a function that returns `Result` or `Option` (or another type that implements `FromResidual`)
 --> src/main.rs:2:34
  |
1 | fn main() {
  | --------- this function should return `Result` or `Option` to accept `?`
2 |     let count: i64 = "70".parse()?;
  |                                  ^ cannot use the `?` operator in a function that returns `()`
  |
help: consider adding return type
  |
1 ~ fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
2 |     let count: i64 = "70".parse()?;
3 |     println!("{count}");
4 +     Ok(())
  |

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0277`.
error: could not compile `kettle_creek` (bin "kettle_creek") due to 1 previous error

In Python you'd write rows = cursor.execute(sql).fetchall() and get a list of tuples. Here you get a Vec of structs whose fields have names and types. That costs you the struct definition, and pays you back every time you type loan. and your editor lists the fields.

Work on the rows

A Vec<T> is Rust's growable list, the equivalent of a Python list whose items all have one type. To count loans that are out:

fn count_out(loans: &[Loan]) -> usize {
    loans.iter().filter(|loan| loan.status == "out").count()
}

.iter() walks the items one at a time without changing or consuming them. .filter(...) keeps the items its closure says yes to, and .count() counts them. Nothing runs until count asks for items. These chains are called iterator adaptors, and they're how most Rust code works through collections. The same thing as a loop:

fn count_out(loans: &[Loan]) -> usize {
    let mut n = 0;
    for loan in loans {
        if loan.status == "out" {
            n += 1;
        }
    }
    n
}

Both compile to essentially the same machine code. Use whichever reads better. Here the chain does: it says "count the out loans" in one line. In Python the chain is sum(1 for loan in loans if loan.status == "out").

Borrowing, in five minutes

Look at the parameter: loans: &[Loan], not loans: Vec<Loan>. The & means count_out borrows the loans: it can read them, and the caller still has them afterwards. This is the idea that makes Rust Rust, so here is what happens without it:

fn total_len(names: Vec<String>) -> usize {
    names.iter().map(|n| n.len()).sum()
}

fn main() {
    let names = vec![String::from("Ada"), String::from("Grace")];
    let n = total_len(names);
    println!("{n} letters across {} names", names.len());
}
error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `names`
 --> src/main.rs:8:45
  |
6 |     let names = vec![String::from("Ada"), String::from("Grace")];
  |         ----- move occurs because `names` has type `Vec<String>`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait
7 |     let n = total_len(names);
  |                       ----- value moved here
8 |     println!("{n} letters across {} names", names.len());
  |                                             ^^^^^ value borrowed here after move
  |
note: consider changing this parameter type in function `total_len` to borrow instead if owning the value isn't necessary
 --> src/main.rs:1:21
  |
1 | fn total_len(names: Vec<String>) -> usize {
  |    ---------        ^^^^^^^^^^^ this parameter takes ownership of the value
  |    |
  |    in this function
help: consider cloning the value if the performance cost is acceptable
  |
7 |     let n = total_len(names.clone());
  |                            ++++++++

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0382`.
error: could not compile `kettle_creek` (bin "kettle_creek") due to 1 previous error

Every value in Rust has exactly one owner. Passing a Vec by value moves it: total_len owns it now, frees it when it returns, and main can't touch it again. Python never has this problem because every variable is a shared reference and a garbage collector cleans up. Rust has no garbage collector. It frees memory at a moment the compiler can see, and ownership is how it sees that moment.

You have three choices whenever a function needs a value:

  • Borrow it (&[Loan], &Loan, &str) when the function only reads. This is the default. Nearly every function you write this week should take its input this way.
  • Borrow it mutably (&mut Vec<Loan>) when the function changes it in place, like sorting.
  • Move it (Vec<Loan>) when the function keeps it or consumes it. Or .clone() it first if you need your own copy, which costs a full copy, every time.

Write &[Loan] rather than &Vec<Loan>. A slice, &[T], is a view of some items in a row, and it accepts a borrowed Vec, an array or part of either. Clippy will tell you this too.

Keep some of the rows

To keep the loans that went out before a date, return a Vec of references to the originals instead of copies. The obvious version doesn't compile:

struct Loan {
    status: String,
    loaned_on: String,
}

fn out_before(loans: &[Loan], cutoff: &str) -> Vec<&Loan> {
    loans
        .iter()
        .filter(|loan| loan.status == "out" && loan.loaned_on.as_str() < cutoff)
        .collect()
}

fn main() {
    let loans = vec![Loan {
        status: "out".into(),
        loaned_on: "2026-08-11".into(),
    }];
    println!("{}", out_before(&loans, "2026-09-01").len());
}

  |                      -------          ----         ^ expected named lifetime parameter
  |
  = help: this function's return type contains a borrowed value, but the signature does not say whether it is borrowed from `loans` or `cutoff`
help: consider introducing a named lifetime parameter
  |
6 | fn out_before<'a>(loans: &'a [Loan], cutoff: &'a str) -> Vec<&'a Loan> {
  |              ++++         ++                  ++              ++

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0106`.
error: could not compile `kettle_creek` (bin "kettle_creek") due to 1 previous error

The function returns references, and the compiler needs to know what they borrow from, so it knows how long they stay valid. Two references come in, so it can't guess. 'a is a lifetime, a name for "as long as this borrow lasts". The suggested fix compiles, but it's stricter than it needs to be: it ties the result to cutoff as well. The results only point into loans, so only loans needs the label:

fn out_before<'a>(loans: &'a [Loan], cutoff: &str) -> Vec<&'a Loan> {
    loans
        .iter()
        .filter(|loan| loan.status == "out" && loan.loaned_on.as_str() < cutoff)
        .collect()
}

Read it as: the &Loans that come out live as long as the loans that went in. Ticket 3 is where lifetimes get properly explained. For now, when the compiler asks, tie the output to the input it really comes from.

loan.loaned_on.as_str() < cutoff compares two pieces of text. as_str() borrows a &str view of the String so both sides have the same type.

Sort

let mut words = vec!["pear", "fig", "kiwi", "apple"];

words.sort_by_key(|w| w.len());
println!("{words:?}");

words.sort_by_key(|w| (w.len(), *w));
println!("{words:?}");

words.sort();
println!("{words:?}");

words.sort_by(|a, b| b.cmp(a));
println!("{words:?}");
["fig", "pear", "kiwi", "apple"]
["fig", "kiwi", "pear", "apple"]
["apple", "fig", "kiwi", "pear"]
["pear", "kiwi", "fig", "apple"]
  • sort_by_key sorts by whatever the closure returns. Sorting changes the Vec, so the variable must be declared let mut. Rust variables can't be changed unless they say so, which is why day one's error happened.
  • The sort is stable: items with equal keys stay in their old order. After the first sort, "pear" still comes before "kiwi" because it did before.
  • A tuple key, (w.len(), *w), sorts by the first part, then breaks ties with the second. Python's key=lambda w: (len(w), w) is the same idea.
  • sort_by takes two items and returns how they compare. b.cmp(a) instead of a.cmp(b) sorts backwards.

Using the pieces together:

println!("out right now: {}", count_out(&loans));

let mut early = out_before(&loans, "2026-09-15");
early.sort_by_key(|loan| (loan.member.as_str(), loan.loan_id));
for loan in &early {
    println!("{} {} {}", loan.member, loan.loan_id, loan.loaned_on);
}
out right now: 3
Alan 3 2026-09-01
Grace 2 2026-08-11

Write a file

use std::fs::File;
use std::io::{BufWriter, Write};

fn write_report(path: &str, loans: &[&Loan]) -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let file = File::create(path)?;
    let mut out = BufWriter::new(file);
    writeln!(out, "loan_id,member,loaned_on")?;
    for loan in loans {
        writeln!(out, "{},{},{}", loan.loan_id, loan.member, loan.loaned_on)?;
    }
    out.flush()?;
    Ok(())
}
loan_id,member,loaned_on
2,Grace,2026-08-11
3,Alan,2026-09-01
  • File::create makes or empties the file. BufWriter collects your small writes in memory and hands them to the operating system in big chunks. Without it, every writeln! is a separate request to the OS, which is much slower.
  • writeln! works like println!, but into anything you can write to. Writing can fail (disk full, no permission), so it returns a Result and needs a ?.
  • flush pushes out whatever is still buffered. A BufWriter also flushes when it's dropped, but it has to ignore errors when it does that. Flushing yourself means an error reaches you.
  • std::io::Result<()> is the I/O module's own Result, with its error type filled in.

Writing CSV by hand works because nothing in this ticket's columns contains a comma. That's a fragile assumption, and ticket 2 replaces it.

Under the hood

Where your data lives: the stack and the heap

A running program gets memory in two places. The stack holds each function's local variables. It is fast, because making room is just moving a pointer, and limited: every value on it must have a size known when the program is compiled. The heap is a big pool for anything else. You ask for a block of any size while running, and someone has to give it back.

A Vec is both. A Vec in a local variable is three numbers on the stack: a pointer to a block on the heap, how many items are in it (length), and how many fit before it needs a bigger block (capacity). The items themselves sit side by side in that heap block. A String has the same three numbers, pointing at bytes of text.

You can measure this yourself:

use std::mem::size_of;
println!("i64:            {} bytes", size_of::<i64>());
println!("String:         {} bytes", size_of::<String>());
println!("Option<String>: {} bytes", size_of::<Option<String>>());
println!("Loan:           {} bytes", size_of::<Loan>());
println!("Vec<Loan>:      {} bytes", size_of::<Vec<Loan>>());
i64:            8 bytes
String:         24 bytes
Option<String>: 24 bytes
Loan:           104 bytes
Vec<Loan>:      24 bytes

A String is 24 bytes whether it holds "Ada" or a novel: the text is elsewhere. And Option<String> costs nothing extra. Some bit patterns can never be a valid String (its pointer is never null, for one), so Rust uses one of those patterns to mean None. The spare pattern is called a niche.

When a Vec runs out of room, it asks the allocator for a bigger block, and today's implementation roughly doubles it. The standard library doesn't promise the factor. The allocator may grow the block where it is, or hand back a new one and copy everything across. Pushing 2,017 IDs one at a time:

let mut ids: Vec<i64> = Vec::new();
let mut last_cap = ids.capacity();
println!("len {:>4}  capacity {:>4}", ids.len(), last_cap);
for id in 0..2017 {
    ids.push(id);
    if ids.capacity() != last_cap {
        last_cap = ids.capacity();
        println!("len {:>4}  capacity {:>4}", ids.len(), last_cap);
    }
}
len    0  capacity    0
len    1  capacity    4
len    5  capacity    8
len    9  capacity   16
len   17  capacity   32
len   33  capacity   64
len   65  capacity  128
len  129  capacity  256
len  257  capacity  512
len  513  capacity 1024
len 1025  capacity 2048

Ten trips to the allocator for 2,017 pushes. Growing by a constant factor means the total copying is at most a small multiple of the final size, so a push costs a constant amount on average, even though the occasional push may copy everything. That's called amortized O(1), and it's the same reason Python's list.append is fast. If you know the size up front, Vec::with_capacity(n) skips the copying entirely. Ticket 7 measures whether that matters.

Moves now make sense too. Moving a Vec copies its 24 bytes and leaves the heap block where it is. What must never happen is two owners both freeing the same block, and that is the mistake the move error stopped.

Why the dates sort as text

println!("{}", "2026-08-11" < "2026-09-01");
println!("{}", "2025-12-31" < "2026-01-01");
println!("{}", "8/11/2026" < "9/1/2025");
true
true
true

Text compares character by character, left to right, and the first difference decides. That's lexicographic order, the way a dictionary is ordered. A YYYY-MM-DD date puts the most significant part first and pads every part to a fixed width, so text order and time order agree. 8/11/2026 breaks both rules, and so it sorts before September 2025. This is why ISO 8601 exists, why your logs and filenames should use it, and why ticket 4, where the dates aren't ISO, needs a real date type.

Engineering wiki / Rust / Grouping and totals

Group by, without SQL

In SQL this is a GROUP BY. In pandas it's df.groupby("supplier_id")["amount"].agg(["count", "sum"]). In Rust you do it yourself with a HashMap, and once you've done it you'll recognize it inside every groupby you ever call.

A map from keys to values

HashMap<K, V> is Python's dict, with one key type and one value type. It lives in std::collections, so it needs a use:

let mut shelves: HashMap<&str, u32> = HashMap::new();
shelves.insert("fiction", 412);
shelves.insert("history", 158);
shelves.insert("fiction", 415); // same key: replaces the old value

println!("{} keys", shelves.len());
println!("{:?}", shelves.get("history"));
println!("{:?}", shelves.get("poetry"));
2 keys
Some(158)
None

get doesn't return the value. It returns an Option: Some(value) if the key is there, None if it isn't. Python's d[key] raises KeyError at run time. Rust makes "the key might not be there" part of the type, so you decide what happens before the program ever runs. Try to skip that decision and the compiler stops you:

use std::collections::HashMap;

fn main() {
    let mut members: HashMap<i64, &str> = HashMap::new();
    members.insert(2, "Grace");
    let name: &str = members.get(&2);
    println!("{name}");
}
error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> src/main.rs:6:22
  |
6 |     let name: &str = members.get(&2);
  |               ----   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ expected `&str`, found `Option<&&str>`
  |               |
  |               expected due to this
  |
  = note: expected reference `&str`
                  found enum `Option<&&str>`
help: consider using `Option::expect` to unwrap the `Option<&&str>` value, panicking if the value is an `Option::None`
  |
6 |     let name: &str = members.get(&2).expect("REASON");
  |                                     +++++++++++++++++

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0308`.
error: could not compile `kettle_creek` (bin "kettle_creek") due to 1 previous error

The suggested .expect("REASON") would compile. It means "crash with this message if the key is missing". That's right when a missing key would be a bug in your program, and wrong when it's something the data can do. Most of the time you want one of these:

match shelves.get("poetry") {
    Some(n) => println!("poetry: {n}"),
    None => println!("no poetry shelf"),
}
if let Some(n) = shelves.get("fiction") {
    println!("fiction: {n}");
}
let poetry = shelves.get("poetry").copied().unwrap_or(0);
println!("poetry, or 0: {poetry}");
no poetry shelf
fiction: 415
poetry, or 0: 0
  • match handles both cases and says what each one does.
  • if let Some(n) = ... is match when you only care about one case.
  • .copied().unwrap_or(0) turns "maybe a reference to a number" into "a number, or 0". copied turns Option<&u32> into Option<u32>. Look up Option in the docs and skim its methods. You'll use a dozen of them by ticket 5.
  • map[&key] also works. It panics if the key is missing, just like Python's d[key]. Use it only where a missing key really is impossible, and you can say why.

Counting and summing: the entry API

The core of every group-by is "find this key's running total, or start one at zero, and add to it". The entry API does that in one lookup:

let words = ["out", "returned", "out", "lost", "out", "returned"];
let mut counts: HashMap<&str, u32> = HashMap::new();
for w in words {
    *counts.entry(w).or_insert(0) += 1;
}
let mut sorted: Vec<(&str, u32)> = counts.into_iter().collect();
sorted.sort();
println!("{sorted:?}");
[("lost", 1), ("out", 3), ("returned", 2)]

counts.entry(w) finds the slot for w. .or_insert(0) fills it with 0 if it's empty and hands back a mutable reference to the value, and the * in front reaches through that reference so += 1 changes the number in the map. .or_default() does the same with the type's default, which is 0 for numbers. Python's version is counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1, or Counter.

A HashMap has no order. To print or write one predictably, collect it into a Vec and sort that. More on why under the hood.

Owned text and borrowed text

Look at the key type: &str, not String. That choice matters more than it looks.

  • String owns its text on the heap. You can keep it as long as you like, change it, and hand it to someone else.
  • &str is a borrowed view of text that somebody else owns: a pointer and a length. It costs nothing to make, but it's only valid while the owner is alive and unchanged.

When your rows are already loaded into a Vec, a map keyed by &str borrows names straight out of those rows, and nothing is copied. A map keyed by String needs its own copy of every key, made with .clone() or .to_string(). For a map that's built, used and thrown away in one function, borrow. For a map that has to outlive the rows it came from, own. The compiler holds you to it:

use std::collections::HashMap;

struct Book {
    title: String,
    shelf: String,
}

fn main() {
    let books = vec![
        Book {
            title: "SICP".into(),
            shelf: "cs".into(),
        },
        Book {
            title: "TAOCP".into(),
            shelf: "cs".into(),
        },
    ];
    let mut per_shelf: HashMap<&str, u32> = HashMap::new();
    for b in &books {
        *per_shelf.entry(b.shelf.as_str()).or_default() += 1;
    }
    drop(books);
    println!("{per_shelf:?}");
}
error[E0505]: cannot move out of `books` because it is borrowed
  --> src/main.rs:23:10
   |
9  |     let books = vec![
   |         ----- binding `books` declared here
...
20 |     for b in &books {
   |              ------ borrow of `books` occurs here
...
23 |     drop(books);
   |          ^^^^^ move out of `books` occurs here
24 |     println!("{per_shelf:?}");
   |                --------- borrow later used here

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0505`.
error: could not compile `kettle_creek` (bin "kettle_creek") due to 1 previous error

per_shelf holds views into books, so books can't be thrown away while per_shelf is still in use. The same program in C would compile, then read freed memory and maybe print garbage. Python never has the problem, because its garbage collector keeps the strings alive as long as anything points at them. Rust rejects it before it runs. Ticket 3 gives this rule its proper name.

The same thinking applies to function parameters. Take &str when you only read text, because a &String turns into a &str automatically and a string literal already is one.

Putting it together

Total fines per library member. Fines belong to loans, and loans belong to members, so it takes two maps: one to look up a loan's member, and one for the running totals.

use rusqlite::Connection;
use snippets::library;
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::error::Error;

struct Loan {
    loan_id: i64,
    member: String,
}

struct Fine {
    loan_id: i64,
    amount: f64,
}

fn load_loans(db: &Connection) -> rusqlite::Result<Vec<Loan>> {
    let mut stmt = db.prepare("SELECT loan_id, member FROM loans")?;
    let rows = stmt.query_map([], |r| {
        Ok(Loan {
            loan_id: r.get(0)?,
            member: r.get(1)?,
        })
    })?;
    rows.collect()
}

fn load_fines(db: &Connection) -> rusqlite::Result<Vec<Fine>> {
    let mut stmt = db.prepare("SELECT loan_id, amount FROM fines")?;
    let rows = stmt.query_map([], |r| {
        Ok(Fine {
            loan_id: r.get(0)?,
            amount: r.get(1)?,
        })
    })?;
    rows.collect()
}

/// Total fines per member, with how many fines each.
fn fines_by_member<'a>(loans: &'a [Loan], fines: &[Fine]) -> HashMap<&'a str, (u32, f64)> {
    let member_of: HashMap<i64, &str> = loans
        .iter()
        .map(|l| (l.loan_id, l.member.as_str()))
        .collect();

    let mut totals: HashMap<&str, (u32, f64)> = HashMap::new();
    for fine in fines {
        let member = member_of[&fine.loan_id];
        let entry = totals.entry(member).or_insert((0, 0.0));
        entry.0 += 1;
        entry.1 += fine.amount;
    }
    totals
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let db = library()?;
    let loans = load_loans(&db)?;
    let fines = load_fines(&db)?;
    let totals = fines_by_member(&loans, &fines);

    let mut rows: Vec<(&str, u32, f64)> = totals
        .into_iter()
        .map(|(m, (n, total))| (m, n, total))
        .collect();
    rows.sort_by(|a, b| b.2.total_cmp(&a.2).then_with(|| a.0.cmp(b.0)));

    for (member, n, total) in &rows {
        println!("{member:<7} {n} fines  {total:>6.2}   (unformatted: {total})");
    }
    Ok(())
}
Ada     3 fines   25.25   (unformatted: 25.25)
Grace   3 fines    1.10   (unformatted: 1.1)
  • member_of is built with .map(...).collect(). Iterators of pairs collect straight into a HashMap.
  • member_of[&fine.loan_id] panics on a missing key. Here every fine was made from a loan, so a missing one would be a bug. In your ticket, think about whether an invoice can name a supplier that isn't in suppliers, and what the report should do if it does.
  • The value is a tuple, (u32, f64): a count and a total, updated through entry.0 and entry.1. A small struct with named fields reads better once there are three or more.
  • fines_by_member has a lifetime 'a on loans and on the output, for the reason you met in ticket 1: the keys of the result are borrowed from loans.

Sorting by a float

The sort line uses total_cmp, not sort_by_key. Here's why:

fn main() {
    let mut totals = vec![("Ada", 25.25), ("Grace", 1.1), ("Alan", 0.0)];
    totals.sort_by_key(|t| t.1);
    println!("{totals:?}");
}

3   |     totals.sort_by_key(|t| t.1);

    |

              i128
              i16

error: could not compile `kettle_creek` (bin "kettle_creek") due to 1 previous error

sort_by_key needs a key that implements Ord, a total order, where any two values compare as less, equal or greater. Floats don't have one, because of NaN ("not a number", what 0.0 / 0.0 gives you). NaN is not less than, equal to or greater than anything, itself included. Python sorts floats anyway and quietly gives you a wrong order if a NaN sneaks in. Rust makes you choose. a.total_cmp(&b) is a total order on floats that puts NaN at the ends, which is what you want for sorting. .then_with(|| ...) breaks ties with a second comparison, just like the tuple keys in ticket 1.

Formatting money

The output above prints each total twice: {total:>6.2} right-aligns it in six characters with two decimals, and plain {total} prints the shortest decimal that reads back as exactly the same float. On this tiny library they agree. On a quarter's invoices they won't, and you'll see digits like ...55000000002. That's not a bug in your code: it's what floating point does. For this report, format with two decimals and move on. Ticket 3 is where it stops being cosmetic.

Writing real CSV

The csv crate handles quoting for you. Any field with a comma, a quote or a line break gets wrapped in quotes, and quotes inside get doubled, which is the rule every spreadsheet program expects:

let mut w = csv::Writer::from_path(&path)?;
w.write_record(["book_id", "title", "fines"])?;
w.write_record(["101", "The Mythical Man-Month", "0.30"])?;
w.write_record(["106", "Programming Pearls, 2nd ed.", "1.10"])?;
w.write_record(["107", "The \"Dragon Book\"", "0.00"])?;
let total = 1.1_f64;
w.write_record(["108".to_string(), "Code".to_string(), format!("{total:.2}")])?;
w.flush()?;
book_id,title,fines
101,The Mythical Man-Month,0.30
106,"Programming Pearls, 2nd ed.",1.10
107,"The ""Dragon Book""",0.00
108,Code,1.10

write_record takes any list of things that look like text, such as string literals or Strings, as long as every field in one record has the same type. That's why the last record turns everything into a String. format! is println! that gives you the String instead of printing it. The csv crate can also write structs directly through serde, but that's more machinery than this ticket needs.

The ticket

Before you type, answer these in your journal. What is the key of your grouping map, and what is the value? Should the key be the supplier's ID or its name, and what goes wrong with names? Do you need the supplier name during grouping, or only when writing? How will you test "July 1 through September 30" at the edges, and is <= "2026-09-30" right for a date written as text?

Stuck?

Hint 1: two maps

One map from supplier ID to name, built from the suppliers. One map from supplier ID to a running count and total, built from the invoices. Group by the ID, which is unique and never misspelled, and look up the name only when you write each row.

Hint 2: from map to sorted rows

Turn the totals map into a Vec with into_iter().collect(), then sort it with sort_by: compare totals with total_cmp (which way round puts the biggest first?), then then_with on the names.

The choices are: skip the invoice (and the total no longer ties to the ledger), keep it under a placeholder name like "(unknown supplier 99)", or stop the program with an error. Which one would Priya want? names.get(&id) gives you an Option to make that choice with.

Under the hood

How a hash table finds things

A HashMap is an array of slots called buckets. To store a key, it runs the key through a hash function, which turns any value into a big number that looks random but is always the same for the same key. Then it uses part of that number to pick a bucket. To find the key again, it hashes it again and looks in the same place. No searching, so lookups take about the same time with ten keys or ten million: O(1) on average.

let buckets = 8;
for member in ["Ada", "Grace", "Alan", "Edsger"] {
    let mut h = DefaultHasher::new();
    member.hash(&mut h);
    let hash = h.finish();
    println!("{member:<7} hash {hash:>20}  bucket {}", hash % buckets);
}
Ada     hash 17390174587215729682  bucket 2
Grace   hash  4016552697901753768  bucket 0
Alan    hash 10154332038248538411  bucket 3
Edsger  hash  6817028703008280599  bucket 7

Two keys can land in the same bucket. That's a collision, and every hash table has a plan for it: look in the next free slot, or keep a little list per bucket. Collisions are why the table keeps spare room. When it gets too full (Rust's table grows when it's seven-eighths full), it allocates a bigger array and moves every key, the same doubling trick as Vec. Rust's HashMap is a port of Google's SwissTable design, which checks sixteen slots at a time with single CPU instructions.

Why the order changes every run

The example above used DefaultHasher::new(), which always hashes the same way, so its output is the same every time. A real HashMap doesn't. Each one gets a hasher with secret random keys, seeded from the operating system. So the same names land in different buckets on different runs, and iterating the map gives a different order.

This is deliberate. If a web server's hash function is fixed and public, an attacker can send thousands of keys built to land in one bucket, and every lookup becomes a slow search through all of them. That's called hash flooding, or HashDoS. In 2011 researchers showed it working against most of the popular web platforms of the day. A secret random key per map stops it, and the hash Rust uses, SipHash, was designed so the keys can't be worked out from outside.

The lesson for your reports: never let output order depend on a HashMap. Sort first. Python's dict keeps insertion order, which hides this habit until you work in a language that doesn't.

Sorting, and what stable means

Comparison sorts, the kind that work by asking "is a before b?", need about n log n comparisons for n items, and it's been proved that none can do better in general. For a report of a couple of dozen rows that's nothing. For ten million rows it's the difference between seconds and hours, compared with a naive sort that needs n².

sort, sort_by and sort_by_key are stable: equal items keep their original order. Since Rust 1.81 they use a merge sort variant called driftsort. sort_unstable and friends can reorder equal items, use no extra memory, and are often faster. Stability matters when you sort twice: sort by name, then stable-sort by total, and suppliers with equal totals stay alphabetical. Your tie-break with then_with gets the same result in one sort, and it says so in the code.

Go deeper

  • The Rust Book, chapter 8.2: Strings and 8.3: Hash Maps.
  • The std::collections docs, especially "When Should You Use Which Collection?" and the table of operation costs.
  • The Option docs. Read the method list once; you'll come back to it.
  • The csv crate's tutorial, by its author, Andrew Gallant. It's a model of how to document a library.
  • Matt Kulukundis, "Designing a Fast, Efficient, Cache-friendly Hash Table, Step by Step", CppCon 2017. The talk that introduced SwissTable. It's about C++, but the ideas are the ones inside Rust's HashMap.
  • Introduction to Algorithms (Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein), chapter 11 on hash tables and chapter 8 on the n log n lower bound for sorting. The standard reference: dense, and worth it in small doses.

Ticket 3: invoices that don't match

From
Dana Whitlock, Operations Manager
To
You

Date
Monday, October 12, 2026, 7:58 AM
Subject
Invoices that don't match their POs

Thanks for the spend report. Priya used it on Thursday's supplier call.

Now the one that matters. Every month we pay a few invoices we shouldn't. Priya's team checks a sample by hand. I want every PO checked against every invoice. Main branch only for now (branch is MAIN): Millbrook's invoices are still in their old system.

What a PO should cost: add up its lines, quantity times unit price.

What we were billed: add up the PO's invoices. One catch. Suppliers sometimes send the same invoice twice and we key in both. If a PO has two invoices with the same invoice number, the one entered later (the higher invoice_id) is a duplicate: don't count it, report it. Two different invoice numbers that add up to the PO's total are fine; some suppliers bill in parts.

Report these, in this order:

  1. ORPHAN_INVOICE: an invoice whose PO number doesn't exist at all. Usually a typo when it was keyed in.
  2. DUPLICATE_INVOICE: the extra copies described above, one row per extra copy.
  3. BILLED_CANCELLED: a cancelled PO with any invoices. We owe nothing on those.
  4. BILLED_OPEN: an open PO that's been invoiced. Shouldn't happen. I want to know if it does.
  5. OVERBILLED: a received PO billed more than it should cost.
  6. UNDERBILLED: a received PO billed less. Often a short shipment, but I still want to see it.
  7. NOT_INVOICED: a received PO with no invoice at all. Suppliers get 30 days, so only POs received on or before September 4.

A received PO billed exactly right isn't on the report.

Send it as discrepancies.csv with columns kind, po_id, invoice_number, supplier, expected, billed, difference:

  • supplier is the name. invoice_number is only filled in on orphan and duplicate rows.
  • expected is what the PO should cost. Put 0.00 for a cancelled PO, and leave it blank on orphan and duplicate rows, where there's nothing to compare.
  • billed is what we were billed for the PO. On an orphan or duplicate row, it's that one invoice's amount.
  • difference is billed minus expected, blank when expected is blank.
  • Money with two decimals, no dollar sign. Sort by kind in the order above, then po_id, then invoice_number.

When it runs, print how many of each kind it found and the total overbilled (the sum of the differences on OVERBILLED rows).

Priya will check your numbers against her sample, to the cent. So to the cent it has to be. The wiki page is here.

Dana

This ticket teaches enums that carry data, exhaustive match, derives, a money type of your own with operator traits, HashSet, Option combinators, let-else and lifetimes properly. Under the hood: how a float stores 0.1, big-O and the hash join, and what a database index is. Crates allowed: rusqlite, csv.

Engineering wiki / Rust / Types that model the business

Make wrong answers hard to write

Ticket 2 was arithmetic. This one is judgment: every PO lands in exactly one of several outcomes, money has to be exact, and three tables have to be lined up against each other. Rust's answer to all three is the same idea: put the rules into types, so the compiler checks them every time you build. The library examples below have the same shapes as the ticket, on different data.

An enum for "exactly one of these"

An enum lists every possible form a value can take. Unlike a Python Enum, each variant can carry its own data:

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
enum Standing {
    Lost,
    Overdue { days: i64 },
    Out,
    Returned,
}

A Standing is Lost, or Overdue with a number of days attached, or Out, or Returned. Never two at once, and never a value that isn't on the list. A string like "overdue" can be misspelled, and the misspelling compiles; Standing::Overdu does not.

You take an enum apart with match:

fn action(standing: Standing) -> String {
    match standing {
        Standing::Lost => "bill the replacement".to_string(),
        Standing::Overdue { days } if days > 30 => format!("{days} days late: send a letter"),
        Standing::Overdue { days } => format!("{days} days late: send a reminder"),
        Standing::Out => "nothing yet".to_string(),
        Standing::Returned => "nothing".to_string(),
    }
}
  • Standing::Overdue { days } matches the variant and pulls its days out into a variable, in one step.
  • if days > 30 after a pattern is a guard: the arm only matches when the condition holds too. Arms are tried top to bottom, so the 40-day loan takes the first Overdue arm and the 3-day loan falls through to the second.
  • A match is an expression. Each arm produces a value, and the whole match is the function's return value.
let mut all = vec![
    Standing::Returned,
    Standing::Overdue { days: 3 },
    Standing::Lost,
    Standing::Out,
    Standing::Overdue { days: 40 },
];
all.sort();
for s in &all {
    println!("{:<26} {}", format!("{s:?}"), action(*s));
}
let late = all
    .iter()
    .filter(|s| matches!(s, Standing::Overdue { .. }))
    .count();
println!("{late} overdue");
Lost                       bill the replacement
Overdue { days: 3 }        3 days late: send a reminder
Overdue { days: 40 }       40 days late: send a letter
Out                        nothing yet
Returned                   nothing
2 overdue

matches!(value, pattern) is a one-line match that answers yes or no. Overdue { .. } means "the Overdue variant, whatever its fields are".

The rule that makes enums worth it: a match must cover every variant. Leave one out and the program doesn't build:

enum Standing {
    Lost,
    Overdue { days: i64 },
    Out,
    Returned,
}

fn action(standing: Standing) -> String {
    match standing {
        Standing::Lost => "bill the replacement".to_string(),
        Standing::Overdue { days } => format!("{days} days late"),
        Standing::Returned => "nothing".to_string(),
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", action(Standing::Out));
}

error: could not compile `kettle_creek` (bin "kettle_creek") due to 1 previous error

This is the compiler keeping a list for you. Add a variant next month and every match that forgot about it becomes an error you have to fix before anything runs. Python's match statement doesn't check this when it runs (a type checker can, if you set it up), and an if/elif chain simply falls off the end. A catch-all arm, _ => ..., turns the check off for that match. Sometimes that's right. In code that decides what to report, it means a new case gets silently reported as nothing.

What each derive buys you

The #[derive(...)] line asks the compiler to write standard behavior for your type. Each one is a trait, a named ability, that other code can rely on:

DeriveWhat you getWhy you'd want it here
DebugPrinting with {:?}Seeing what you have while you work
Clone, Copy.clone(); and with Copy, plain assignment copies instead of movingSmall values like a kind or an amount should behave like numbers. Copy is only allowed when every field is Copy, so not for a String
PartialEq, Eq== and !=Comparing kinds and amounts
PartialOrd, Ord<, .cmp(), .sort()For an enum the order is the order you declared the variants in. That's why Lost sorted first above
HashUsable as a HashMap key or in a HashSetCounting per kind
DefaultA zero value, T::default()What entry(...).or_default() starts from

Declaration order as sort order is worth noticing. If your report must list kinds in a set order, declare the enum's variants in that order and derive Ord: then sorting is correct by construction, and nobody has to keep a separate list of strings in step with the enum.

Why PartialEq and Eq are two things: floats. f64 has NaN, which isn't equal even to itself, so f64 can only be PartialEq. And because it isn't Eq or Hash, it can't be a HashMap key:

use std::collections::HashMap;

fn main() {
    let mut by_price: HashMap<f64, &str> = HashMap::new();
    by_price.insert(0.30, "loan 4");
    println!("{:?}", by_price.get(&0.30));
}

That's the type system hinting that floats and exact comparison don't mix. The next section shows why.

Money is not a float

The library stores fines the way our warehouse system stores prices: as REAL dollars. Loan 1 has two fines, 10 and 20 cents. Loan 4 has one fine of 30 cents. Add them up in f64:

let mut stmt = db.prepare("SELECT loan_id, amount FROM fines")?;
let fines: Vec<(i64, f64)> = stmt
    .query_map([], |row| Ok((row.get(0)?, row.get(1)?)))?
    .collect::<Result<_, _>>()?;

let mut owed: HashMap<i64, f64> = HashMap::new();
for (loan_id, amount) in &fines {
    *owed.entry(*loan_id).or_default() += amount;
}
println!("loan 1 owes {}", owed[&1]);
println!("loan 4 owes {}", owed[&4]);
println!("same amount? {}", owed[&1] == owed[&4]);
println!("loan 7 owes {}", owed[&7]);
println!("printed nicely: {:.2} and {:.2}", owed[&1], owed[&7]);
loan 1 owes 0.30000000000000004
loan 4 owes 0.3
same amount? false
loan 7 owes 0.7999999999999999
printed nicely: 0.30 and 0.80

Thirty cents is not thirty cents. {:.2} hides the problem when you print, which is why ticket 2's totals looked fine. It doesn't help when you compare, and this ticket is nothing but comparisons. Under the hood explains where the stray digits come from. The fix is the one every payments system uses: turn the float into whole cents once, the moment it leaves the database, and never do arithmetic on money as a float again.

Make cents a type of its own, a struct with one unnamed field. A wrapper like this is called a newtype:

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, Default, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
struct Cents(i64);

impl Cents {
    /// The one place a float becomes money: round to the nearest cent, once.
    fn from_dollars(dollars: f64) -> Cents {
        Cents((dollars * 100.0).round() as i64)
    }
}

The .0 reaches the field inside. Why not just use i64? Because then a quantity, an ID and an amount are all i64, and adding a PO number to a price compiles. With Cents, the compiler only lets money combine with money.

A new type starts with no abilities except the derived ones. You add the rest by implementing standard traits. Display is what {} uses:

impl fmt::Display for Cents {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
        write!(f, "{}.{:02}", self.0 / 100, self.0 % 100)
    }
}

And Add is what + uses:

impl Add for Cents {
    type Output = Cents;

    fn add(self, other: Cents) -> Cents {
        Cents(self.0 + other.0)
    }
}

type Output = Cents says what Cents + Cents produces. Now the fines again, in cents:

let mut owed: HashMap<i64, Cents> = HashMap::new();
for (loan_id, amount) in &fines {
    let total = owed.entry(*loan_id).or_default();
    *total = *total + Cents::from_dollars(*amount);
}
println!("loan 1 owes {}", owed[&1]);
println!("loan 4 owes {}", owed[&4]);
println!("same amount? {}", owed[&1] == owed[&4]);
println!("loan 7 owes {}", owed[&7]);
loan 1 owes 0.30
loan 4 owes 0.30
same amount? true
loan 7 owes 0.80

Two more traits will make your code read better, and writing them is yours to do:

  • AddAssign is +=. With it, *total = *total + x becomes *total += x. One method, add_assign(&mut self, other: Cents).
  • Sum lets an iterator of Cents end in .sum(). Its one method takes an iterator and folds it, starting from Cents(0). Look at Iterator::fold.

Before you trust the Display above with your report, try it on negative amounts, because difference is often negative:

println!("{}", Cents(-150));
println!("{}", Cents(-5));
-1.-50
0.-5

Integer division and remainder keep the sign, so both halves come out negative. Fixing it is part of the ticket. Two hints: print the sign yourself, and look up i64::unsigned_abs.

Indexes: find things without searching

Ticket 2 used a HashMap to add things up. Here it does its other job, an index: build it once, then jump straight to any item by its key. The map holds references into a Vec you already have, so nothing is copied:

let by_id: HashMap<i64, &Book> = books.iter().map(|b| (b.book_id, b)).collect();

let mut borrowed_before: HashSet<i64> = HashSet::new();
for loan in &loans {
    let Some(book) = by_id.get(&loan.book_id) else {
        println!(
            "loan {}: no book {} in the catalog",
            loan.loan_id, loan.book_id
        );
        continue;
    };
    let again = !borrowed_before.insert(book.book_id);
    println!(
        "loan {}: {}{}",
        loan.loan_id,
        book.title,
        if again { " (again)" } else { "" }
    );
}
loan 1: The Mythical Man-Month
loan 2: Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs
loan 3: The Art of Computer Programming
loan 4: The Mythical Man-Month (again)
loan 5: A Discipline of Programming
loan 6: Notes on the Synthesis of Form
loan 7: The Art of Computer Programming (again)
loan 8: no book 999 in the catalog
  • HashMap<i64, &Book> maps a book ID to a borrowed book. Building it is one pass over books.
  • let Some(book) = ... else { ... }; is let-else. If the pattern matches, book exists for the rest of the loop body. If not, the else block runs, and it must leave: continue, return or break. It keeps the normal path flat instead of nesting it inside an if let.
  • A HashSet<T> is a HashMap with keys and no values: a fast "have I seen this?". insert returns false when the item was already there, so one call both checks and records. A set's key can be a tuple, such as (i64, String), when "the same" means two fields at once.

map.get(&key) returns an Option, and Option has methods that save you writing a match each time:

let title = |id: i64| {
    by_id
        .get(&id)
        .map(|b| b.title.as_str())
        .unwrap_or("(unknown)")
};
println!("{}", title(104));
println!("{}", title(999));

let copies: HashMap<i64, u32> = HashMap::from([(101, 2), (103, 1)]);
let n = |id: i64| copies.get(&id).copied().unwrap_or_default();
println!("copies of 101: {}, of 105: {}", n(101), n(105));
A Discipline of Programming
(unknown)
copies of 101: 2, of 105: 0
MethodWhat it does
.map(|x| ...)Changes the value inside a Some; leaves None alone
.copied()Turns Option<&u32> into Option<u32>, for Copy types
.unwrap_or(x)The value, or x if None
.unwrap_or_default()The value, or the type's Default: 0 for numbers, empty for strings
.is_some_and(|x| ...)true only if there's a value and it passes the test

Lifetimes, properly this time

Ticket 1 met 'a on a function. An index is the same idea in a struct: a Catalog that holds references must say how long they're good for.

struct Catalog<'a> {
    by_id: HashMap<i64, &'a Book>,
}

impl<'a> Catalog<'a> {
    fn new(books: &'a [Book]) -> Catalog<'a> {
        Catalog {
            by_id: books.iter().map(|b| (b.book_id, b)).collect(),
        }
    }

    fn title(&self, id: i64) -> Option<&'a str> {
        self.by_id.get(&id).map(|b| b.title.as_str())
    }
}

Read Catalog<'a> as "a catalog that borrows something for the span 'a". new says the catalog borrows from books, and title says the text it hands back comes from the books too, not from the catalog, so it stays valid even after the catalog is gone.

let books = vec![
    Book {
        book_id: 101,
        title: "The Mythical Man-Month".to_string(),
    },
    Book {
        book_id: 104,
        title: "A Discipline of Programming".to_string(),
    },
];
let catalog = Catalog::new(&books);
println!("{:?}", catalog.title(104));
println!("{:?}", catalog.title(7));
Some("A Discipline of Programming")
None

Now the mistake everyone makes once: a helper that loads the books and returns the catalog.

use std::collections::HashMap;

struct Book {
    book_id: i64,
    title: String,
}

struct Catalog<'a> {
    by_id: HashMap<i64, &'a Book>,
}

impl<'a> Catalog<'a> {
    fn new(books: &'a [Book]) -> Catalog<'a> {
        Catalog {
            by_id: books.iter().map(|b| (b.book_id, b)).collect(),
        }
    }

    fn title(&self, id: i64) -> Option<&'a str> {
        self.by_id.get(&id).map(|b| b.title.as_str())
    }
}

fn load_catalog<'a>() -> Catalog<'a> {
    let books = vec![Book {
        book_id: 101,
        title: "The Mythical Man-Month".to_string(),
    }];
    Catalog::new(&books)
}

fn main() {
    let catalog = load_catalog();
    println!("{:?}", catalog.title(101));
}
error[E0515]: cannot return value referencing local variable `books`
  --> src/main.rs:29:5
   |
29 |     Catalog::new(&books)
   |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^------^
   |     |            |
   |     |            `books` is borrowed here
   |     returns a value referencing data owned by the current function

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0515`.
error: could not compile `kettle_creek` (bin "kettle_creek") due to 1 previous error

books belongs to load_catalog, so it's freed when load_catalog returns. The catalog would point at memory that no longer holds books. In C this compiles and crashes later, or worse, doesn't crash and reads garbage. Rust refuses. There are two honest fixes:

  • Own the data higher up. Load the Vec in main (or whoever needs the answer), then build indexes that borrow from it. The data lives at the top, and everything below borrows. This is the usual shape, and the right one for this ticket.
  • Let the index own its data: a HashMap<i64, Book> with no references and no lifetime. Fine when the index is the only place the data lives.

The fix that isn't honest is .clone() sprinkled until the errors go away. It works, it copies everything, and it hides the question of who owns what, which is the question this ticket's design depends on.

In src/bin/drills.rs, as before.

The ticket

Still one program in src/main.rs. It will be long; that's fine for now, and ticket 4 is where it gets split up. You will need the csv crate from ticket 2 again.

Before you type, draw the data flow in your journal. Which tables come in, and which indexes do you build from them? (There are at least three: what each PO should cost, what each PO was billed, and the invoice numbers already seen on each PO.) What owns the data, and what only borrows it? Which kinds come from looking at invoices one at a time, and which from looking at POs? What should difference be on a NOT_INVOICED row? And one trap: the house rule bans ORDER BY, and SQL without ORDER BY promises no particular row order. So how do you know which copy of a duplicate was entered later?

Stuck?

Hint 1: two passes

Walk the invoices once, in invoice_id order, and you can settle the orphans and duplicates and add up what each PO was billed. Then walk the POs once and decide each one's kind from its status, its expected total and its billed total. Each pass is a single loop with index lookups inside it.

Hint 2: one row type for every kind

Every report row has the same columns, so make one struct for a row, with a field for the kind. The blanks are Options: expected: Option<Cents> is None on orphan and duplicate rows. Then difference doesn't need to be stored at all; it's a method that maps over expected.

Hint 3: matching on two things at once

You can match on a tuple, and combine patterns with guards. Look up std::cmp::Ordering: billed.cmp(&expected) gives you Less, Equal or Greater, which is an enum too, so it can sit in a pattern next to the PO's status. If your status is still a String, that's a sign it wants to be an enum as well.

Sanity checks

These confirm your loading and your setup, not the answer.

  • 5,315 PO lines and 1,745 invoices loaded. 1,711 POs are on the main branch with status received.
  • 89 POs have more than one invoice row. That's split billing and duplicates together, so it's not your duplicate count.
  • If you compare dollar totals as f64 with ==, 508 of the 1,649 received main-branch POs that have invoices look mismatched. If your over and under counts add up to anything near 508, there's a float in your comparison. Most of those 508 are not real.
  • Check one row by hand. Pick an OVERBILLED PO from your file and look at it with sqlite3: SELECT * FROM po_lines WHERE po_id = ...; and the same for invoices. Do the sum on paper. Using SQL to look is allowed.
  • Run it twice. The file should be byte for byte the same both times (cmp or diff will tell you). If it isn't, something is coming out of a HashMap unsorted.
